paper_metadata.title: Longitudinal assessment of local and global functional connectivity following sports-related concussion

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study clearly defines the target population (NCAA Division I athletes) and uses a relevant control group (healthy contact-sport athletes) to account for the athletic setting. Inclusion/exclusion criteria and recruitment methods are well-documented.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: NCAA Division I student-athletes (N = 94) were referred by sports-medicine professionals
items.reasoning: The population is specifically identified as elite collegiate athletes, which is the target for sports-related concussion research.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Physicians trained in sports medicine diagnosed concussions independently of the study at the time of injury following recommend guidelines (McCrory et al. 2013)
items.reasoning: Recruitment relied on clinical referral following standardized diagnostic guidelines, reducing selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the follow-up intervals (T1, T2, T3) are described, the calendar years or duration of the total recruitment period are not explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location) are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: NCAA Division I student-athletes... approved by an institutional review board. [Affiliations: Medical College of Wisconsin, University of New Mexico, Laureate Institute for Brain Research]
items.reasoning: The setting (Division I athletics) and the specific academic/research institutions involved are clear.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: All participants self-reported no past or current mood disorders, anxiety disorders, alcohol abuse, or substance abuse... Physicians trained in sports medicine diagnosed concussions... based on a clinical exam assessing symptoms, a cranial nerve check, manual muscle testing...
items.reasoning: Both psychiatric exclusion criteria and the clinical diagnostic criteria for the concussion (the 'zero time' event) are detailed.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: NCAA Division I student-athletes (N = 94) were referred by sports-medicine professionals
items.reasoning: The text does not state how many athletes were eligible but declined to participate, making it impossible to calculate a participation rate.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Demographic information for all participants... can be found in Table 1. [Age, Education, Gender, Previous Concussions, Sport, Medication, ADHD, LOC, PTA]
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive breakdown of relevant baseline characteristics for both groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: There is notable attrition over the three time points (from 34 at T1 to 30 at T3 for imaging, and even lower for behavioral data). While the authors use Linear Mixed-Effects models to handle missing data, the characteristics of those lost to follow-up are not explicitly compared to those who completed the study.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Forty-three concussed athletes participated in at least one of three visits... Nineteen concussed athletes participated in all three visits and 36 participated in at least 2 visits.
items.reasoning: Only 44% (19/43) of the concussed sample completed all three visits, which is a significant drop-off for a longitudinal study.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not describe efforts to re-engage or collect data from those who missed subsequent visits.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper notes that 'not every participant was able to complete every visit' but does not provide specific reasons (e.g., withdrawal, scheduling, or symptom severity).

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no table or text comparing the baseline characteristics of dropouts versus completers.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Because the characteristics of dropouts are not reported, it is impossible to determine if attrition was informative (biased).

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (concussion) was diagnosed by independent professionals using established clinical guidelines. The imaging metrics (ReHo and GBC) are well-defined and processed using standard, validated neuroimaging pipelines.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Physicians trained in sports medicine diagnosed concussions independently... based on a clinical exam assessing symptoms, a cranial nerve check, manual muscle testing... Rhomberg's test... King-Devick test.
items.reasoning: The 'exposure' (concussion) is defined by a multi-modal clinical assessment.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Physicians trained in sports medicine diagnosed concussions independently of the study at the time of injury following recommend guidelines (McCrory et al. 2013)
items.reasoning: Diagnosis was made by experts independent of the research team using international consensus guidelines.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: ReHo is the Kendall's coefficient of concordance for a time series... Pearson correlation between time series data from each voxel with all other voxels was calculated, Fisher z-transformed
items.reasoning: The study uses continuous metrics for connectivity rather than arbitrary thresholds.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: MRI was performed using a General Electric Healthcare Discovery MR750 3-Tesla whole body MRI scanner... Participants were instructed to fixate on a cross
items.reasoning: All participants underwent the same standardized imaging protocol on the same scanner.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: fcMRI [usable data]: T1=28, T2=29, T3=26 [from N=43 enrolled]
items.reasoning: A significant number of scans were excluded due to motion or artifacts (e.g., only 28/43 at T1), though this is common in fMRI.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Linear mixed-effects (LME) models with time as a fixed factor and a random intercept to account for missing data were used
items.reasoning: LME is a standard and appropriate statistical method for handling missing data in longitudinal designs without requiring simple imputation.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a mix of objective (ANAM) and subjective (HAM-D/A) outcomes. A major concern is the lack of blinding for the clinical mood assessments, which the authors acknowledge as a potential source of rater bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Structured interviews for the Hamilton Depression (HAM-D) and Anxiety (HAM-A) Rating Scales served as the primary behavioral measures.
items.reasoning: The primary outcomes are standardized clinical scales with clear definitions.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: However, structured interviews were not conducted blinded to concussion status and thus rater bias cannot be ruled out.
items.reasoning: While the tools (HAM-D/A) are valid, the lack of blinding for the interviewer introduces potential measurement bias.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics 4 Sports Medicine Battery (ANAM) was used to collect secondary measures... Structured interviews... served as the primary behavioral measures.
items.reasoning: The same battery of tests and interviews was applied to all participants across all time points.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounts for some confounders (age, education, previous head hits via the control group), but there is a significant difference in the number of prior concussions between the groups. While the authors performed supplementary analyses for ADHD, they did not fully adjust the primary models for the baseline difference in prior concussion history.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1: Age, Education, Gender, Previous Concussions, Sport, Health/Medication, ADHD
items.reasoning: The study tracks the most relevant confounders for this population.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Previous Concussions: 0.93 (1.14) [CA] vs 0.59 (1.10) [HA]
items.reasoning: While the number of concussions is listed, the severity or specific timing of prior injuries is not detailed.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: All participants self-reported no past or current mood disorders... number of prior concussions and the number of censored time points were square root transformed
items.reasoning: Confounder data (like prior concussions) relied on self-report, which is subject to recall bias.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Demographic information for all participants... can be found in Table 1.
items.reasoning: Data collection was standardized for both groups.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not specify how missing demographic or confounder data were handled, though LME was used for the main analysis.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: A sample of healthy contact-sport collegiate athletes served as controls to account for potential confounds associated with collegiate athletics
items.reasoning: The use of contact-sport controls is a strong design choice, but the groups were not perfectly matched on prior concussion history.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: concussed athletes had more prior concussions than HA... supplementary analyses indicated that local connectivity differences remained largely unchanged when excluding [ADHD] subjects
items.reasoning: While they checked for ADHD, they did not explicitly include 'prior concussions' as a covariate in the primary voxel-wise LME models despite the group difference.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach is robust, using Linear Mixed-Effects models for longitudinal data and appropriate Monte Carlo simulations to correct for multiple comparisons in the imaging data. The results are reported transparently, including null findings for GBC.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise LMEs were performed using the AFNI program 3dLME... Monte Carlo simulations (10,000 iterations) determined the necessary correction for familywise error rate
items.reasoning: The analytical steps for both behavioral and imaging data are clearly documented.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Linear mixed-effects (LME) models with time as a fixed factor and a random intercept to account for missing data were used
items.reasoning: The model choice is appropriate for the longitudinal, repeated-measures design.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: The estimated smoothness of the residuals... Monte Carlo simulations... p < 0.05 for all voxel-wise analyses
items.reasoning: The use of LME and rigorous cluster-size correction for fMRI data is standard and adequate.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Contrary to our hypothesis, no significant cross-sectional or longitudinal differences in GBC were observed.
items.reasoning: The authors report their null findings regarding GBC, which suggests a lack of reporting bias.
